**Streaming delivers partial output before the response is complete.** It improves perceived responsiveness, but it introduces a distinction between “some bytes arrived” and “the task completed successfully.” The application must preserve that distinction in its state. [1](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/)

Consider a response intended to be `{"total": 42}`. The client may initially receive `{"to`, then more fragments. A network event is not necessarily a whole JSON value, token, or user-visible character. Use the transport's framing rules and an incremental buffer; do not parse every fragment as a complete final object.

Track a terminal reason such as normal completion, length limit, cancellation, or transport failure. A length-limited response can be syntactically incomplete or omit important qualifications. Even if the text looks plausible, it should not silently receive the same status as a fully completed answer.

Cancellation needs propagation. When a user closes the request, the client should stop rendering, the server should signal the inference worker, and the worker should release generation resources according to its capabilities. Merely dropping the browser connection can leave expensive generation running in the background. Confirm this behavior with measurements, since support varies by serving stack.

For structured outputs and external actions, validate the complete result before execution. A partially streamed tool argument is not an authorized final action. If the stream fails after an external write, reconcile its state rather than assuming nothing happened and repeating it. Idempotency and request identifiers help with this recovery. [1](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/)[3](https://research.google/pubs/the-ml-test-score-a-rubric-for-ml-production-readiness-and-technical-debt-reduction/)

Measure time to first token and total completion latency separately. Streaming can make the first metric feel better without reducing the second. Test interruption at arbitrary fragment boundaries, malformed frames, missing terminal events, and client cancellation. Those checks establish whether the UI and backend agree about completion and resource ownership, which is more useful than a demo that only exercises a perfect network connection.
